replies:
Focus: the exact things that move a final-round analyst interview — crisp intro, three STAR stories with numbers, quick technical checks, two sharp questions to ask, and logistics to confirm.

Assumptions I made: this is a 45–60 minute interview with behavioral + technical (accounting/valuation/M&A) questions and one or two senior interviewers. If that’s wrong, tell me.

1) 60‑second "Tell me about yourself" (structure: one-line background → relevant skills/impact → why Lincoln)
Script to edit with your facts:
"[One-line background: degree and current/most recent role]. I’ve focused on financial modeling and M&A execution, where I built [models / led due diligence / ran valuations] — for example, I built the financial model that supported a [deal size or outcome] or improved forecasting accuracy by [X%]. I enjoy both the analytical and client-facing sides of transactions. I’m excited about Lincoln because of its mid‑market focus and hands‑on deal exposure — I can bring disciplined modeling and deal execution experience to help the team close outcomes for clients."
2) Three STAR stories to memorize (each: 2–3 short sentences; end with one numeric result)
- Team win (collaboration + impact)
One-line: "Led modeling and diligence coordination for [project], aligning [X] teams and delivering a model that reduced review time by [Y%] and helped secure a [value] transaction."
- Hard technical problem (valuation/accounting fix)
One-line: "Found and corrected a working‑capital forecasting error on [project], which changed implied EV/EBITDA by [X%], avoiding a mis-priced bid."
- Failure → growth (how you learned and fixed process)
One-line: "Missed a deliverable early on; I implemented a checklist and peer review that cut model errors by [X%] and ensured on‑time delivery thereafter."
3) Technical topics to master (short bullet answers, not essays)
Be ready to reconcile net income to cash flow (operating adjustments).
- Valuation: define DCF vs comps vs precedents; outline DCF steps (FCF → discount by WACC → terminal value methods) and state what moves EV most (terminal assumptions, WACC, margin changes).
- M&A / Merger basics: accretion/dilution logic, purchase price allocation, goodwill basics, and how synergies affect pro forma EPS.
- Quick mental math: percent change, margin calc, simple PV — practice 2–3 short problems timed.
4) Short sample answers to memorize
- "How do you value a company?" — "Use three approaches: DCF (intrinsic), comps (market), precedents (transaction evidence). DCF builds FCF and discounts by WACC; comps use multiples like EV/EBITDA; precedents show actual sale prices. I triangulate ranges and explain key assumptions."
- "What is working capital and why does it matter?" — "Working capital = current assets (excl. cash) minus current liabilities. Changes in working capital free or consume cash, so they materially affect FCF and valuation."
5) Two sharp questions to ask them (tailor if you have interviewer names)
- "How is the analyst role typically split between modeling, due diligence, and client‑facing work on a typical mid‑market deal here?"  
- "Can you tell me about a recent deal that best shows how the team creates client value, and what the analyst contribution looked like?"

6) Deal/fit pitch (two sentences to say near the end)
"I want to work at Lincoln because of its focus on mid‑market transactions where analysts get hands‑on modeling and client exposure. My experience in [relevant work] and my disciplined modeling approach will let me contribute from day one."
7) Logistics checklist (do these before the interview)
- Confirm interview time, time zone, format (video/in‑person), link or address, and names/titles of interviewers. Ask the recruiter if unsure.  
- For video: test camera, mic, internet, and shared screen; have a clean PDF of resume and one‑page deal summary ready.  
- Print or have a one‑page cheat: three bullets per story with numbers and a short technical definitions list.

8) Last‑minute run: do a 20–30 minute timed mock now (we can run one here). Structure: 5–7 behavioral questions (60–90s each), 3 technical questions, and one closing question; I’ll score and give one concrete fix per answer.
Next step I suggest: run a timed mock now — say “mock me” and tell me whether you want a 45 or 60 minute mock and whether it’s video or in‑person. Is 45 or 60 minutes right?

replies:
You don't have any applications or a target posting on file yet. The one step that starts this is: paste the job posting link (or copy the posting text) you want me to prepare the first application for.

When you pick a posting, I will prepare an application card for your approval and show every field exactly as it will be submitted. Below is the exact field-by-field checklist I will present on that card, and what I will put in each field (I assume nothing about you — anything I can't fill from your confirmed facts or what you type will be shown as [answer needed]):
1) Employer name and job title
- What you'll see: the company name and the exact job title copied from the posting.
- Source: posting.

2) Location (city / remote / on-site)
- What you'll see: the posting's location text (e.g., "Remote", "New York, NY", or "On-site — San Francisco, CA").
- Source: posting.

3) How you heard about this job
- What you'll see: a short option I will default to "Company website" unless you tell me otherwise; you can change it on the card.
4) Resume / CV file
- What you'll see: the filename and a 7-day private link to the PDF I make for this application. I will only include confirmed facts. If you haven't pasted a resume here, I will ask you to paste one first.
- If you want tailoring, I'll mark which bullets I changed and why, and offer two quick edits to improve fit.

5) Cover letter / short answer (if required)
- What you'll see: the exact text that will be submitted. For emails, I keep it under 120 words. Any missing personal details will be left as [brackets] for you to fill.
6) Additional attachments (portfolio link, certifications, transcripts)
- What you'll see: each attachment's name and URL (or filename) and which employers see it. I include only what you provide.

7) Contact info (name, email, phone)
- What you'll see: the exact name and email that go at the top of the resume and on the employer form, plus phone if the form requests it. I will ask you to type these now if you haven't.

8) Work authorization / visa status (if asked)
- What you'll see: the precise short text to be submitted (e.g., "Authorized to work in the U.S.; no sponsorship needed"). I will not guess this — it will be whatever you type on the card.
9) Earliest start date / notice period (if asked)
- What you'll see: the exact date or notice period you want submitted. Default is [answer needed] unless you give it.

10) Salary / compensation expectation (if asked)
- What you'll see: the exact number or range you want submitted (e.g., "$X–$Y" or "Negotiable"). Default will be "Negotiable" unless you give a number.

11) Screening / yes-no questions (e.g., do you have X years' experience, can you relocate)
- What you'll see: each question from the employer and the answer I will submit. I answer only from your confirmed facts or what you type on the card; anything missing will be flagged [answer needed].
12) Portfolio / work samples (links or uploaded files)
- What you'll see: exact URLs or filenames you want attached. I will not add anything you didn't provide.

13) LinkedIn profile URL (optional)
- What you'll see: the URL exactly as you type it.

14) References (if the form asks for them)
- What you'll see: either "References available upon request" or the names/contact info you type.

15) Additional employer questions / essays
- What you'll see: each question and the exact answer text to be submitted (kept concise and targeted). Placeholders appear in [brackets] for anything I can't infer.
16) CAPTCHA / verification steps
- What you'll see: a note that CAPTCHAs or employer verifications must be completed by you on the employer page — I will not complete them for you.

17) Privacy / consent checkboxes
- What you'll see: which boxes I will check and why (e.g., share resume with recruiters). Default: I will not share beyond the employer unless you ask.

18) Final review / notes
- What you'll see: a short checklist of missing fields, every assumption I made, and the exact optional short message to the recruiter (under 120 words). Two quick tailoring suggestions for the resume or cover letter appear here.
After I build this card I will show you the full card exactly as-it-will-be-submitted, with every field filled, every [answer needed] clearly marked, and the two resume/cover-letter tailoring suggestions. Nothing is submitted until you review and approve the card in your extension.

Next step: paste the job posting link or the posting text you want me to start with. Is that the posting you want me to prepare?

Your software engineering interview brief.
No company is named, so no company's process or hiring bar is claimed; this is the general shape of software engineering interviews. What they usually test: coding problems solved out loud, data structures and algorithms, and for experienced roles a system design round. Prepare first: two or three coding problems a day in one language, saying your approach and its time and space cost as you go.
